excerpt: Introduction Claude Code and Codex can both use your computer. Under the hood they work in a similar manner: both can give the model a screenshot and an accessibility tree, a text description of every button on screen, and let it click by position or by naming an element. The text version of the screen was built decades ago, for people who couldn’t see it. In 1984, two IBM mathematicians, Jim Thatcher and his former thesis adviser, Jesse Wright, who was blind, started a side project to read the PC’s screen out loud. When GUIs turned the screen into pixels, apps had to start describing themselves instead. Microsoft shipped Active Accessibility in 1997, Sun started AT-SPI for Linux in 2001, and Apple added its Accessibility API in 2002. This text has been useful for agents too. Models looking only at screenshots completed about one task in twenty on the 2024 OSWorld benchmark, whereas most models reading the screen as text performed better. How do those results hold up with stronger models? We tested screenshots on their own and with the accessibility tree on seven models, and used the results to decide how our QA agent, TREX, should see the screen. What's so hard about clicking a button? A person clicks a button by moving the mouse to it. A model, on the other hand, looks at a screenshot and has to write the coordinates out as text (e.g., ‘x=523, y=217’) before clicking on it. Getting these numbers off by a few pixels can mean it clicks the wrong thing. The same button sits at different coordinates on different screen and window sizes, so the guesses get worse when the resolution changes. Also, the model’s vision works against it as it doesn’t see a screenshot pixel by pixel. The image is initially shrunk to fit the model's size limit, then cut into tiny squares, each dozens of pixels wide. But a click still has to land on one exact pixel. Small targets are hard.
